title: India Leads the Wilderness in Tiger Conservation

PIB Backgrounder

India Leads the Wilderness in Tiger Conservation

“Protecting Tigers, Preserving Ecosystems”

प्रविष्टि तिथि:
28 JUL 2026 11:01AM by PIB Delhi

India has emerged as a global leader in tiger conservation through science based policies and strong institutional support. The country is now home
to nearly 70%
of the world's wild tigers. Technology driven monitoring, effective governance and community participation have strengthened conservation outcomes. India is also advancing global cooperation to secure the future of tigers and their habitats.



Thriving Tigers, Resilient Ecosystems

International Tiger Day, observed every year on
29 July
, highlights the global importance of tiger conservation. For India, it reaffirms the Government's long-standing commitment to science-based conservation and sustainable development. The day also showcases India's remarkable conservation achievements. Today, India is home to the
world's largest wild tiger population
, accounting for nearly
70% of
all wild tigers globally
. This success reflects decades of sustained policy support, scientific management and community participation, positioning India as a global leader in tiger conservation.

This achievement is rooted in India's deep cultural and ecological connection with the tiger. For centuries, ancient coins, royal seals and temple carvings have portrayed the tiger as a symbol of strength and sovereignty. Recognising this enduring legacy, the Government declared the
Royal Bengal Tiger
 as the National Animal in
1972
. Today, the tiger continues to represent India's rich biodiversity, ecological wealth and shared natural heritage across diverse landscapes.

Beyond its cultural significance, the tiger plays a vital ecological role. As an apex predator and umbrella species, it helps maintain healthy forest ecosystems. Conserving tiger habitats protects forests, rivers and countless other species. These forests regulate water, conserve soil, support pollination and moderate local climates. They also reduce disaster risks and provide ecosystem services that sustain rural livelihoods and urban economies. By protecting tigers and their habitats, the Government is strengthening biodiversity conservation, enhancing ecological security and advancing the vision of
Viksit Bharat
 through sustainable development.

Did You Know?
International Tiger Day traces its origins to the
Saint Petersburg Tiger Summit held in November 2010
. Leaders from 13 tiger-range countries, including India, adopted the ambitious Tx2 goal to double the global wild tiger population by 2022. Today, it serves as a global platform to review conservation progress, strengthen international cooperation and raise awareness. In 2010, only about 3,200 wild tigers were estimated to remain globally. By 2022, improved conservation and scientific monitoring increased the estimate to around 4,500, with a plausible range of 3,700–5,600 tigers.
According to recent global estimates, approximately 5,711 wild tigers remain worldwide, representing an increase of around 78% since 2010.



Rise in the Tiger Numbers: From Crisis to Recovery

India's tiger conservation efforts have emerged as a global model of wildlife recovery.

The country has more than doubled its scientifically assessed tiger population since 2006. The
All India Tiger Estimation (2022)
 places India's tiger population at
3,682
. The
2022 All India Tiger Estimation
 covered
20 States
 and surveyed over
6.41 lakh kilometres
 on foot. It is among the world's largest and most comprehensive wildlife assessments. This remarkable recovery reflects sustained policy support, science-based conservation and strong institutional governance. Long-term habitat protection, rigorous monitoring and coordinated implementation continue to strengthen tiger conservation across India.

Robust Governance Architecture for Tiger Conservation

India’s policy framework for tiger conservation combines long term vision with sustained institutional support at national and state levels. Project Tiger, the National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) and Tiger Conservation Plans together provide a robust, science based governance architecture for tiger habitats.

Project Tiger

Project Tiger is a flagship Centrally Sponsored Scheme of the Government of India. It is implemented by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC). The scheme aims to secure viable tiger populations in their natural habitats. It provides financial and technical assistance to tiger range States for conservation efforts. The programme combines habitat protection, scientific management and regular field based monitoring. This approach has strengthened conservation measures over time.

According to the
National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) Report (2023)
, Project Tiger has established a network
of 58 tiger reserves

across
18 tiger-range States
. These reserves cover around
84,500 square kilometres
, which is about
2.56% of India's geographical area
. Today, Project Tiger remains a cornerstone of India's wildlife conservation efforts and reflects the Government's long term commitment to protecting tigers and their habitats.

Did You Know?
 Section 38 V (3)
 of the Wildlife Protection Act, (WPA), 1972 requires every State Government to prepare a Tiger Conservation Plan for each tiger reserve. Such plans must ensure protection of tiger reserves and provide habitat inputs to maintain viable populations of tigers, co predators and prey animals

National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA)

NTCA oversees the implementation of
Project Tiger
 and related conservation initiatives. NTCA provides scientific, technical and financial guidance to tiger range States. It approves Tiger Conservation Plans and issues standard operating procedures for reserve management. The Authority also monitors the management of tiger reserves through periodic assessments. Its science based approach improve habitat protection, improves conservation outcomes and supports the long term survival of wild tigers across India.

Did You Know?
NTCA is chaired by the Union Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change. It also includes Members of Parliament, senior government officials and experts. The Authority guides tiger conservation, oversees tiger reserves and ensures effective implementation of Project Tiger across the country.



Tiger Task Force

The Government of India constituted the Tiger Task Force to re-examine conservation policies and recommend reforms. The
Tiger Task Force
 reviewed India's tiger conservation framework and recommended key policy reforms. It brought together administrative experts, ecologists and community representatives. The Task Force emphasised transparency, community participation and stronger institutional support for
Project Tiger
. Its recommendations shaped a more robust conservation framework. They led to significant amendments to the
Wildlife (Protection) Act
 in
2006
. The amendments established the
National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA)
and the
Wildlife Crime Control Bureau (WCCB)
 as statutory bodies.

India's tiger conservation framework reflects a strong governance model built on institutions and cooperative federalism. This integrated approach is helping secure the future of tigers while advancing India's biodiversity.

Did You Know?
 India's tiger reserves follow a
landscape-based conservation approach
. Each reserve includes a
Core Area
 (also known as Critical Tiger Habitat) and a
Buffer Area
. Core Areas receive the highest level of protection. Buffer Areas balance conservation with sustainable livelihoods. Also,
Wildlife corridors
 connect tiger reserves, enabling safe movement and maintaining healthy tiger populations across landscapes.

Monitoring and Evaluation of Tigers in India

India has developed a robust, science-based system to monitor and evaluate its tiger population. The approach combines field surveys, camera traps, digital technologies and scientific analysis. It generates reliable data on tiger populations, prey species and habitat quality. This information guides evidence-based conservation planning and adaptive management. Continuous monitoring strengthens habitat protection and enables informed management decisions across tiger landscapes.



All India Tiger Estimation
(AITE)
:

The World's Largest Biodiversity Survey

AITE
 is the world's largest biodiversity survey. Conducted every four years, it is led by the
NTCA
 in collaboration with the
Wildlife Institute of India (WII)
. It estimates tiger populations, co-predators, prey species and habitat quality across all tiger bearing States. The
2022 assessment
 also included India's first nationwide survey of ungulates. The exercise highlighted the importance of healthy prey populations for sustaining viable tiger populations.

Did You Know?
 The
All India Tiger Estimation
 is recognised as the
world's largest biodiversity survey
. The
NTCA's camera trap survey
 also holds a
Guinness World Record
 as the world's largest camera trap wildlife survey. Together, advanced technologies and scientific monitoring make India's tiger estimation among the most rigorous in the world.



Technology Driven Monitoring

India has integrated advanced digital technologies into every stage of tiger monitoring.  The
Monitoring System for Tigers – Intensive Protection and Ecological Status (M-STrIPES)
 uses GPS, GPRS and remote sensing technologies for field monitoring. GPS tagged photographs improve data accuracy and reduce human error. The platform integrates field observations into a central database for scientific analysis and informed decision making. Artificial intelligence further strengthens monitoring. The
Camera Trap Data Repository and Analysis Tool (CaTRAT)
 automatically classify camera trap images by species.
 ExtractCompare
 identifies individual tigers using their unique stripe patterns. Collectively, these tools improve the accuracy and reliability of tiger population estimates.

Management Effectiveness Evaluation (MEE)

The
MEE
 assesses how well tiger reserves are managed. The framework evaluates planning, protection, management processes and conservation outcomes. It helps identify management gaps and reinforce accountability. By
2022
,
51 tiger reserves
 had been evaluated under the framework.
Twelve reserves
 received
"Excellent"
 ratings, while the average management score reached
78%
. The findings guide policy decisions, strengthen reserve management and support long-term conservation planning.

India's Global Leadership in Tiger Conservation

India is actively collaborating with countries across the world to strengthen tiger and wildlife conservation. Key partnerships include transboundary biodiversity conservation with
Nepal and Bhutan
. Collaboration with
Myanmar
 focuses on combating timber trafficking and conserving tigers and other wildlife. India also cooperates with
Russia
on camera trap data management and through the
Indo-Russia Working Sub-Group on Tiger
 and Leopard Conservation. Partnerships with
Botswana, South Africa, Guatemala, Cambodia,
 Kenya and Namibia strengthen wildlife conservation, management and sustainable biodiversity use. India has also established bilateral cooperation with China on tiger conservation. These partnerships reinforce India's commitment to global wildlife conservation through science, cooperation and shared action.

International Big Cat Alliance (
IBCA)



IBCA is a global coalition of
95 big cat range and partner countries
, scientific organisations and conservation partners. The Alliance promotes cooperation for conserving
seven big cats
—tiger, lion, leopard, snow leopard, cheetah, jaguar and puma. The
Union Cabinet
 approved its establishment on
12 March 2024
,
 with its Secretariat headquartered in
India
. Building on India's globally recognised tiger conservation experience, the IBCA strengthens international collaboration to protect big cats and their habitats.

Global Tiger Forum (GTF)

GTF is the world's only intergovernmental organisation dedicated exclusively to tiger conservation.
Headquartered in New Delhi
, it brings together
13 tiger range countries
-Bangladesh, Bhutan, Cambodia, China, India, Indonesia, Lao PDR, Malaysia, Myanmar, Nepal, Russia, Thailand and Vietnam. The Forum promotes a common approach to conserving tigers, their prey and habitats. It supports landscape-scale conservation, regional capacity building and technological innovation to strengthen tiger conservation across member countries. Through knowledge sharing and international cooperation, the GTF reinforces India's leadership in global tiger conservation.

Integrated Tiger Habitat Conservation Programme (ITHCP)

ITHCP is the
International Union for Conservation of Nature's (IUCN)
 flagship tiger conservation initiative. It is funded by the German Government through KfW Development Bank. The programme supports science-based conservation projects across priority tiger landscapes in Asia. It promotes habitat protection, landscape level conservation and international collaboration.
India
actively participates in ITHCP programmes, strengthening regional efforts to conserve tigers and their habitats.

Did You Know?
Conservation Assured Tiger Standards
CA|TS is a global certification system that ensures effective management specifically of tiger conservation areas. Launched at the
1st Asian Parks Congress in Japan in 2013
. It sets benchmarks for protection, habitat management, community involvement, and wildlife monitoring. CA|TS supports efforts to create safe, sustainable environments for tigers and preserve global biodiversity.
CA|TS has accredited 23

Indian tiger reserves ensuring

global best practices in conservation
.



India's international partnerships are strengthening collective action for tiger conservation across borders. By sharing knowledge, technology and best practices, India continues to advance global efforts to protect tigers and their habitats.

Towards a Secure Future for Tigers

Tiger conservation remains a dynamic and evolving priority for the India. Looking ahead, India’s vision is to secure connected, climate resilient tiger landscapes that support both wildlife and people. Continued investment in data driven monitoring, technology- enabled protection and capacity building of frontline staff will support this vision. Cooperation with other tiger range countries and global partners will also help share knowledge and reinforce collective conservation gains. International Tiger Day offers a recurring opportunity to engage citizens, particularly youth, in this forward looking agenda. By combining strong policy direction with sustained implementation, India aims to keep its tiger conservation journey on a path of global leadership.
